'''war-flame''' (wâr′flām), ''n.'' A bale-fire used signal in time of war, as of the approach c enemy. See ''bale-fire'' and ''bale''<sup>2</sup>.

'''war-fork''' (wâr′fôrk), ''n.'' A weapon, use Europe in the middle ages, consisting metal fork with several prongs made fas the end of a long pole.

'''war-horse''' (wâr′hôrs), ''n.'' '''1.''' A horse used l mounted soldier or officer in battle; especia in a somewhat poetical sense, the horse c knight or commander. Compare cuts un ''caparisoned'' and ''muzzle.''

'''warison†''' (war′i-so̤n), ''n.'' [< ME. ''warison'', ''warisoun'', ''wareson'', < OF. ''warison'', ''guarison'', ''garison'', guard, protection, < ''warir'', guard: see ''warish''.] '''1.''' Healing.—'''2.''' Protection.
{{smaller block|War thoru hym & ys men in fair ''wareson'' he broghte.
{{right|''Rob. of Gloucester'', p. 11}}}}
'''3.''' Reward; guerdon; requital.
{{smaller block|<poem>And thus his ''warisoun'' he took
For the lady that he forsook.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 1538}}
<poem>Ho wol winne his ''wareson'' now wiȝtly him spede
Forto saue my sone.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2379}}
<poem>He made a crye thoroowt al the tow[n],
Whedur he be zoman or knave,
That cowthe brynge hym Robyn Hode,
His ''warisone'' he shuld haue.</poem>
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Monk'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 14)}}}}
'''4.''' Erroneously, in the following passage, a note of assault.
{{smaller block|<poem>Either receive within thy towers
Two hundred of my master’s powers,
Or straight they sound the ''warrison'',
And storm and spoil thy garrison.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iv. 24.}}}}

readings.c3s1:
New Zealanders.

'''warlaw†''', ''n.'' An obsolete variant of ''warlock''<sup>1</sup>.

'''warld''' (wärld), ''n.'' A Scotch form of ''world.''

'''warlike''' (wâr′līk), ''a.'' '''1.''' Fond of war; easily provoked to war; ready to engage in war; fit or prepared for war; martial: as, a ''warlike'' nation.
{{smaller block|She . . . made her people by peace ''warlike.''
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}
'''2.''' Of or pertaining to war; martial; military.
{{smaller block|<poem>They were two knights of perelesse puissaunce,
And famous far abroad for ''warlike'' gest.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ii. 16.}}
<poem>The great archangel from his ''warlike'' toil
Surceased.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 257.}}}}
'''3.''' Betokening or threatening war; hostile.
{{smaller block|The ''warlike'' tone again he took.
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, v. 19.}}}}
'''4.''' Having a martial appearance; having the qualities of a soldier; befitting a soldier.
{{smaller block|By the buried hand of ''warlike'' Gaunt.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 3. 109.}}}}

'''warling†''', ''n.'' [Appar. a word coined to rime with ''darling'' (see def.), either < ''war''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>, meaning ‘one often ''warred'', contended, or quarreled with,’ or perhaps < ''warry'', curse, + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] A word occurring only in the proverb “Better be an old man’s darling than a young man’s ''warling,''” ''Camden'', Remains.

'''warlock<sup>1</sup>''' (wâr′lok), ''n.'' [Also ''warluck;'' a Sc. form, preserving the orig. guttural (the reg. mod. E. form would be *''warlow''), < ME. ''warloghe, warlaghe, werlaghe, warlow, warlowe, warlaw, warlawe,'' < AS. ''wǣrloga'' (= OHG. ''wārlogo''), a traitor, deceiver, liar, truce-breaker, < ''wǣr,'' a covenant, truce, compact, the truth (cf. ''wǣrleás,'' truthless, false), + *''loga,'' a liar, < ''leógan'' (pp. ''logen''), lie: see ''very'' and ''lie''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1†.''' A deceiver; a truce-breaker; a traitor.
{{smaller block|<poem>Quen fundin was this hali crois,
the ''warlaghe'' saide on-loft with vois.</poem>
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 121.}}}}
'''2.''' A person in league with the devil; a sorcerer; a wizard.
